question: When can discarding easy or hard examples improve a learner trained on labels from an imperfect generator, and can one theory explain both aggressive reasoning-data curation and protection against recursive synthetic-data collapse?

key_findings.claim: The paper derives an exact high-dimensional classification-error formula in which a symmetric curation rule enters through four scalar moments.
key_findings.evidence: For isotropic Gaussian covariates and squared-loss ridge regression on generator labels, Theorem 1 expresses limiting 0/1 test error through deterministic equivalents of a pruned Marchenko-Pastur resolvent. The retained fraction p and moments gamma, beta, and beta-tilde summarize the curation rule; Theorem 3 reuses the formula after modifying those moments for a label-correctness filter.

key_findings.claim: In a nested data-rich, unregularized, near-perfect-oracle limit, the optimal margin filter switches with generator quality: retain small-margin examples for a perfect generator and large-margin examples for an imperfect one.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 2 uniquely selects the paper's 'keep hard' rule as generator and oracle alignment approach one, but selects 'keep easy' for fixed generator alignment below one as oracle alignment approaches one. This is an asymptotic statement after d,n grow, regularization vanishes, and d/n then vanishes; it is not a finite-data neural-network guarantee.

anchors.section: Appendix L.1, proof of the non-label-aware optimum

key_findings.claim: The synthetic validation does not directly validate the stated estimator and its reported grid description is internally unclear.
key_findings.evidence: The theory defines a squared-loss ridge estimator, and the appendix later says the plotted classification estimator is computed with SciPy linear algebra. Yet Appendix B says the 15-configuration validation trains logistic regression at lambda=1e-6. Its listed Cartesian factors—three n values, three p values, four generator angles, and two policies—describe far more than 15 settings without specifying which 15 were used. Fifty-run confidence intervals therefore validate an incompletely specified, apparently different objective.

anchors.section: Appendix B, coverage and agreement protocol
Appendix B, Figure 4 and statistical checks

key_findings.claim: The paper's operational meanings of 'easy' and 'hard' reverse across sections, making a central empirical label ambiguous.
key_findings.evidence: Section 2.2 calls large absolute margins easy and neighborhoods of the decision boundary hard, and Appendix M encodes KE as |t| above a threshold and KH as |t| below it. Appendix C.3 instead calls the neighborhood of zero 'very easy' and the tails 'very hard'; Figure 8 likewise calls the largest projections the hardest/most informative examples. These are opposite definitions, not a cosmetic notation change.

anchors.section: Appendix C.3, Equations 20-21 and difficulty labels

key_findings.claim: The LLM argument is a post-hoc interpretation of other papers rather than an experiment that measures the theory's generator-quality variable.
key_findings.evidence: The AIME tables are explicitly aggregated from LIMO, s1, and Sun et al. The authors label the same base model a strong generator on average questions and a weak generator on a hard slice, but do not estimate rho, oracle quality, margin distributions, selection propensities, or a counterfactual keep-easy versus keep-hard intervention on that model.

anchors.section: Section 6, claimed unification and future text evaluation

key_findings.claim: The ImageNet experiments report a data-scale crossover and reduced pseudo-label collapse, but do not isolate unique-data curation from repetition or expose the selection mechanism well enough to reproduce it.
key_findings.evidence: Figures 2-3 report keep-easy superiority from 160K initial examples, keep-hard superiority from 1.2M, and stability across pseudo-label rounds when hard valid examples are retained. Appendix A fixes total iterations by increasing epochs inversely with dataset fraction, so smaller curated sets are repeated more. It names ViT-B/16, AdamW, 32 H100s, and augmentation, but never gives the operational score, thresholds, retained counts per round, seeds, error bars, or independent selection/evaluation splits for the central curves.

anchors.section: Section 4.3, ImageNet setup and crossover claim
Appendix A, dataset and training setup

key_findings.claim: Neither the theory nor the empirical design identifies causal data value or establishes transfer across model size.
key_findings.evidence: The theory ranks examples using projections correlated with a ground-truth direction and, in the label-aware case, filters using oracle correctness. Such association can predict utility without identifying the effect of retaining a sample under randomized selection. ImageNet uses one architecture and the LLM section has no new model runs; no scaling test across parameter counts, no prospective bucket randomization, and no uncertainty over neural training runs is reported.

anchors.section: Section 6, future nonlinear and broader evaluation

key_findings.claim: The regression extension shows that aggressive projection-based selection can mitigate a stylized label-shift error, but it also exposes the danger of carrying the paper's natural-language curation story across tasks.
key_findings.evidence: Theorems 4-5 characterize regression risk and reduce optimal symmetric pruning to a three-interval rule; Figure 8 reports an advantage after controlling for the pruned sample count. However, the figure's largest-projection examples are labeled hard while the classification setup labels those examples easy, so this extension does not provide a consistent semantic bridge from margin geometry to real-data difficulty.

method.core_idea: Represent data curation as a symmetric binary function of a sample's projection onto an oracle direction, then use random-matrix deterministic equivalents to calculate the downstream error of a linear learner trained on labels produced by a possibly misaligned generator.
method.mechanism: Gaussian inputs are labeled by a generator vector while test labels follow a ground-truth vector. A label-agnostic rule keeps examples from their projected margin; a label-aware rule additionally requires agreement with an oracle label. Alignment cosines quantify generator, pruner, and ground-truth quality. The curation function's moments enter an exact limiting ridge-risk formula, which is optimized in data-rich limits and compared with synthetic simulations, literature-derived AIME numbers, and pseudo-labeled ImageNet training.
assumptions: Inputs are high-dimensional Gaussian and the main presentation is isotropic; train/test difference is reduced to linear label shift.
The learner is squared-loss ridge regression even though the task metric is classification error.
The curation function is symmetric in a one-dimensional oracle projection and selection dependence is summarized by a few moments.
Label-aware curation can query whether a generator label agrees with a hidden oracle label.
The strongest optimality result takes nested infinite-data and vanishing-regularization limits and an excellent pruning oracle.
Geometric alignment rho is treated as generator quality and margin magnitude as example difficulty.
The mapping from this linear geometry to neural vision and language curation is assumed rather than derived.
ImageNet validation accuracy is treated as unaffected by reuse frequency even though small curated datasets receive more epochs.

techniques.role: Encodes keep-easy, keep-hard, or more general symmetric selection as a binary function of an oracle projection.
Retains only examples whose generated label agrees with an oracle before applying the difficulty filter.
Reduces pruned high-dimensional ridge risk to resolvent limits and four curation moments.
Uses pairwise cosines among generator, oracle, and ground-truth directions as quality parameters.
Uses a pretrained ImageNet model as generator and pruner across repeated pseudo-labeling rounds.
Recasts published AIME results as strong- versus weak-generator regimes without a new LLM intervention.

evaluations.setting: Gaussian linear classification with d=200 across sample sizes, pruning fractions, generator angles, and keep-easy/keep-hard policies.
evaluations.metric: Angular or 0/1 classification error, relative discrepancy from theory, and 95% confidence intervals over 50 runs.
evaluations.result: The appendix reports 1.8% mean relative error, all discrepancies below 5%, and theory inside the confidence intervals.
evaluations.baseline: Analytic asymptotic curves; the claimed logistic-regression implementation conflicts with the squared-loss estimator and the 15 selected configurations are not enumerated.

evaluations.setting: Four synthetic regimes crossing n in {100,5000} with perfect versus imperfect generator quality.
evaluations.result: Keeping all data wins in both small-data settings and with the poor generator; aggressive hard-example pruning wins only for abundant data with a perfect generator.
evaluations.baseline: Equal-size random selection using an orthogonal uninformative pruner.

evaluations.setting: Published AIME average and hard-slice results from LIMO, s1, and Climbing the Ladder of Reasoning.
evaluations.metric: Pass@1 or Avg@8 versus cited training-set size.
evaluations.result: Small curated sets look favorable on average AIME, while hard-level results generally rise with larger datasets.
evaluations.baseline: Cross-paper table comparison; models, evaluation metrics, curation pipelines, and compute are not controlled, and rho is never measured.

evaluations.setting: ImageNet-1K pseudo-label training with ViT-B/16 initialized from either 160K or 1.2M examples.
evaluations.result: The plotted optimum crosses from keep-easy at small initial data to keep-hard at full-scale initial data.
evaluations.baseline: Ground-truth-label and pseudo-label curves, but no seed-level uncertainty, selection details, or prospective threshold protocol.

evaluations.setting: Multiple rounds of ImageNet pseudo-label self-training.
evaluations.result: Training on all pseudo-labels degrades while a hard-and-valid subset is plotted as stable.
evaluations.baseline: All-example self-training; no clean-data mixing, deduplication, memorization, per-round retained count, or independent repeats are reported.

evaluations.setting: Compute and scale audit of the ImageNet experiment.
evaluations.metric: Training iterations, epochs, hardware, and model family.
evaluations.result: Total optimizer iterations are held fixed and training uses 32 H100 GPUs, but epochs rise inversely with dataset fraction and only ViT-B/16 is tested.
evaluations.baseline: Compute is approximately iteration-matched, while unique-token exposure, exact image reuse, and parameter-count transfer are not matched or tested.

limitations: The principal theorem is a Gaussian linear, squared-loss, high-dimensional asymptotic result; neural feature learning, nonlinearity, optimizer dynamics, and representation-dependent difficulty are outside it.
Optimal keep-easy/keep-hard conclusions require a data-rich unregularized limit and an excellent oracle, but finite-data recommendations are stated more broadly.
The label-aware rule assumes access to oracle correctness, which is precisely the expensive or unavailable quantity in many synthetic-data pipelines.
The synthetic appendix says logistic regression while the theory and later implementation text specify a least-squares estimator.
The stated 15-setting synthetic protocol does not identify which points were selected from the much larger listed product grid.
ImageNet's hard/easy scoring function, thresholds, retained counts, pseudo-label loop, seeds, and error bars are omitted.
Holding iterations fixed makes small datasets repeat more, confounding curation, unique-data quantity, and memorization.
No deduplication or train-validation near-duplicate audit is given, including across recursively pseudo-labeled rounds.
The LLM section measures neither generator quality nor the proposed margin and compares results across papers rather than running a controlled intervention.
There is no model-size transfer test, no neural scaling law, and no finite-sample uncertainty for the deep experiments.
Margin correlation and oracle agreement are predictive selection variables, not randomized causal estimates of a sample's marginal training value.
The paper contradicts itself about whether near-zero or tail projections are easy, so difficulty-based recommendations are not implementation-safe as written.
failure_modes: If a practitioner follows the appendix's difficulty labels instead of Section 2, the intended keep-easy and keep-hard policies are exchanged.
A pruner correlated with evaluation labels can create selection/evaluation leakage and make curation look useful without generalizing to a new target distribution.
An imperfect correctness oracle can preferentially delete rare valid modes, improving average accuracy while worsening support and tail behavior.
Equal-step training on a smaller subset can overfit repeated images or benefit from extra epochs, falsely attributing the change to which examples were selected.
A base model can be strong on average and weak on a slice, but assigning rho post hoc makes the theory unfalsifiable unless quality thresholds are fixed prospectively.
Projection margin in a linear Gaussian model may invert or lose its relation to semantic difficulty after neural representation learning.
Near-perfect-theory agreement can survive an implementation mismatch when both are tuned or evaluated on a selected subset of configurations.
Pseudo-label collapse mitigation on one model and validation set may fail at larger model sizes, longer recursive chains, or duplicate-heavy corpora.
reusable_insights: Data value should be modeled conditionally on learner state and generator competence rather than as a universal example ranking.
A curation study should cross randomize example bucket and training stage, reserve an untouched evaluation set, and report prospective treatment effects rather than only correlations with margins.
Curation comparisons need both token/step-matched and unique-data-matched controls because repetition is itself an intervention.
Operational definitions of difficulty require automated invariance tests that catch reversed threshold conventions across theory, code, and captions.
Synthetic theory validation should run the exact estimator in the theorem and enumerate every configuration before inspecting results.
Recursive synthetic-data evaluation should measure tail support, duplicate memorization, calibration, and downstream slice performance in addition to average accuracy.
Generator quality should be estimated on a preregistered calibration split and then tested prospectively across model sizes and data scales.
open_questions: Does the keep-easy/keep-hard crossover persist under neural feature learning once compute, repetition, and retained-data size are independently controlled?
Can a noisy verifier's false-positive and false-negative rates be incorporated without assuming access to oracle correctness at selection time?
What learner-state observable predicts the crossover prospectively better than simple loss, confidence, or margin?
How does curation change semantic support and rare-mode coverage rather than only classification error?
Do randomized bucket interventions recover the same ordering as the paper's alignment correlations, or are those rankings non-causal?
How do deduplication, exact reuse count, dataset size, and model size jointly alter recursive pseudo-label collapse?
Can the theory be extended to a consistently defined difficulty measure in kernels, random features, or finite-width neural networks?

competitive_landscape.title: Beyond neural scaling laws: beating power law scaling via data pruning
competitive_landscape.difference: Sorscher et al. derive pruning-induced scaling predictions and benchmark ten pruning metrics on CIFAR-10, SVHN, and ImageNet. The reviewed paper adds imperfect generated labels, oracle correctness, and model-collapse framing, but its deep validation is less operationally specified and its optimality remains a narrower Gaussian limit.
competitive_landscape.source_version: arXiv v6 primary record and abstract checked 2026-08-23

competitive_landscape.title: LIMO: Less is More for Reasoning
competitive_landscape.difference: LIMO reports strong math performance after supervised fine-tuning on a very small strategically designed dataset and proposes a cognitive-template hypothesis. It does not instantiate the reviewed paper's Gaussian margins or estimate rho, so its results are motivating observations rather than validation of the theory.
competitive_landscape.source_version: arXiv v3 primary record and abstract checked 2026-08-23

competitive_landscape.title: s1: Simple test-time scaling
competitive_landscape.difference: s1 validates difficulty, diversity, and quality criteria for a 1,000-example reasoning set and couples fine-tuning to budget forcing at inference. The reviewed paper cites its small-data result but does not model diversity, trace quality, or test-time compute and runs no controlled replication of s1's curation choices.
competitive_landscape.source_version: arXiv v3 primary record and abstract checked 2026-08-23

competitive_landscape.title: Beyond Model Collapse: Scaling Up with Synthesized Data Requires Verification
competitive_landscape.difference: Feng et al. theoretically characterize imperfect verification in Gaussian-mixture linear classification and test it on transformer eigenvalue computation and LLM summarization. The reviewed paper generalizes correctness-only verification with a difficulty filter, but assumes a near-perfect oracle for its sharp optimum and provides no comparable language-model intervention.
competitive_landscape.source_version: arXiv v2 primary record and abstract checked 2026-08-23

competitive_landscape.title: Model Collapse Demystified: The Case of Regression
competitive_landscape.difference: Dohmatob et al. derive high-dimensional regression formulas and adaptive-regularization mitigation for recursive model collapse. The reviewed paper extends this analytic family to projection-based data curation and classification, but inherits the same linear asymptotic gap and does not compare pruning against tuned regularization in its neural experiments.
competitive_landscape.source_version: arXiv v2 primary record and abstract checked 2026-08-23

competitive_landscape.title: Strong Model Collapse
competitive_landscape.difference: Strong Model Collapse studies how even small synthetic fractions can break scaling and explicitly varies random-projection model size, with language and image experiments. The reviewed paper proposes curation as mitigation but does not test whether its policy survives the model-size-dependent amplification identified there.
competitive_landscape.source_version: arXiv v2 primary record and abstract checked 2026-08-23

competitive_landscape.title: The Curse of Recursion: Training on Generated Data Makes Models Forget
competitive_landscape.difference: Shumailov et al. demonstrate tail loss under recursive generated-data training in VAEs, Gaussian mixtures, and language models. The reviewed paper focuses on linear label shift and average classification error, so it does not directly test preservation of rare modes—the central failure mode in the earlier work.
competitive_landscape.source_version: arXiv v3 primary record and abstract checked 2026-08-23

competitive_landscape.title: On the Stability of Iterative Retraining of Generative Models on their own Data
competitive_landscape.difference: Bertrand et al. prove stability when the initial generator is accurate enough and each generation retains sufficient clean data, then validate normalizing flows and diffusion models. This is an alternative intervention—clean-data mixing rather than selective pruning—that the reviewed ImageNet recursion experiment does not benchmark.
competitive_landscape.source_version: arXiv v5 primary record and abstract checked 2026-08-23

competitive_landscape.title: Climbing the Ladder of Reasoning: What LLMs Can-and Still Can't-Solve after SFT?
competitive_landscape.difference: Sun et al. stratify AIME24 into difficulty tiers and find that curated small data offers limited advantage while larger SFT sets better address hard problems. The reviewed paper reinterprets those observations through unmeasured generator quality; it does not causally compare dataset size with difficulty selection under one fixed model and budget.
competitive_landscape.source_version: arXiv v2 primary record and abstract checked 2026-08-23

novelty_assessment.author_claim: A unified random-matrix theory explains when aggressive hard-example curation beats scaling, when easy examples are preferable for weak generators, and why curation can prevent model collapse.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The exact pruned-risk formula and generator-dependent asymptotic optimum are genuine extensions of data-pruning and linear-collapse analyses, accompanied by synthetic and ImageNet illustrations.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The strongest novelty is the conditional linear-theory crossover, not a validated general law of neural or LLM curation. Priority is narrowed by Sorscher-style pruning, verification-based collapse mitigation, and existing small-data reasoning systems; reversed difficulty definitions, estimator mismatch, under-specified ImageNet selection, and post-hoc LLM interpretation materially weaken the practical claim.

reviewer_notes: All 38 PDF pages, including experimental appendices and proofs, were read. Claims were separated into author reports, reviewer inferences, and contradiction audits. The audit explicitly checked selection/evaluation leakage, theory-to-neural extrapolation, compute/iteration matching, unique-data reuse, deduplication and memorization omissions, finite-sample uncertainty, model-size transfer, oracle dependence, and causal-versus-correlational data value. Nine unique competitor primary records were independently opened through official arXiv records; repositories are treated only as possible implementation contexts and are not mapped to this paper.
